In his Journal, under 28 November 1942, André Gide discusses the deliberate scuttling of the French fleet at Toulon.
A classic example of suicide in the face of a choice that is inwardly impossible but forced upon you by circumstances.
Neither East nor West, neither Germany nor England, was possible for the French fleet.
Is that not Germany’s entire situation today? And if Toulon were to serve as our model, would we not have to commit suicide too?
Gide says of the decision made by the French officers—to sink their ships rather than serve either the British or the Germans:
“It meant placing honor above even the interests of the fatherland … and despite everything, there is in this a preference for oneself over the cause, which leaves the conscience uneasy.”
What a kitsch phrase from such a demanding stylist, a man who is usually merciless when he finds weaknesses like this in the great authors!

“One admires,” he says, “but one cannot approve. In the terrible dead end into which they had put themselves, they had no choice left except suicide or servitude. There was no possible escape, no way out. From the moment our fleet failed immediately to choose dissidence, it became either useless or dishonored. Submission to the terms of the armistice amounted to a delayed scuttling. At the side of the English, this fleet could have rendered very great services”—that is: they would have stood on the side of the victor. Shame on you for this morality after the event, old man!
—“it now serves only as an example of the harm caused by obedience once personal conscience no longer assents to the orders it receives.”
Every sentence in this argument would have to be analyzed. It would be worth doing, because the situation of Germany—indeed, of Europe—is the same today.
Here lies the true moral problem beneath the choice between East and West.
What Gide offers is prophecy turned backward. It is the viewpoint of the victor. It means giving up one’s own French existence.
In a situation like this, suicide is the escape: voluntary destruction rather than serving victors with whom one cannot identify.
Gide argues in the most naive possible way, like a historian without dialectics.
